one_liner: Google's OpenSSL fork, the TLS and crypto library of Chrome and Android; only weak, mixed evidence that it beats OpenSSL on RSA/ECDSA.
what_it_does: A libcrypto plus libssl pair (TLS 1.2/1.3, QUIC hooks, X.509, RSA, ECDSA/ECDH on P-224 to P-521, X25519/Ed25519, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) that keeps OpenSSL's C API shape for the subset it retains. PORTING.md describes it as mostly source-compatible with OpenSSL 1.1.0 (and largely 1.0.2), with removed APIs and BoringSSL-specific additions; code that uses the retained EVP_*, RSA_*, EC_KEY_* and SSL_* calls usually ports with little change. It is consumed live-at-head: projects pin a git revision, link it statically and update it regularly; there are no supported release branches.
how_it_is_fast: Most hot paths share lineage with OpenSSL's perlasm (CRYPTOGAMS) assembly: Montgomery-multiplication bignum code for RSA, and the Gueron-Krasnov nistz256 P-256 code (x86-64 and AArch64, with MULX/ADCX/ADOX variants and a 148 KiB precomputed base-point table, dropped under OPENSSL_SMALL). Elsewhere it uses Fiat Cryptography generated field arithmetic (P-256 on other targets, Curve25519), some CryptOpt-optimized assembly, and VAES/VPCLMULQDQ AES-GCM in AVX2 and AVX-512 versions (aes-gcm-avx2-x86_64.pl, aes-gcm-avx512-x86_64.pl). RSA keys cache their BN_MONT_CTX after first use, so repeated operations on a long-lived key skip that setup. No documented algorithmic advantage over OpenSSL for RSA or ECDSA was found; any edge comes from removed code and different tuning.
when_to_use: You embed TLS in an application or service that already pins and statically links its dependencies, and can update BoringSSL from git head on a regular schedule (the Chromium/Android model).
You need P-256 ECDHE/ECDSA, X25519 and AES-GCM handshake and record throughput from a mature, heavily fuzzed and audited stack rather than from a single-primitive research library.
You want post-quantum TLS key exchange (ML-KEM) and ML-DSA/SLH-DSA in the same library that already ships in Chrome.
You need a smaller API surface than OpenSSL 3.x (no providers, no OCSP client library, fewer legacy ciphers), which also shrinks the attack surface.
AES-128-GCM bulk throughput on recent x86-64: one third-party run (aws-lc issue 2283, Zen 3) measured BoringSSL at about 1.8x AWS-LC at 16 KB records.
when_not_to_use: As a system or distribution library, or behind a stable ABI: the README says it is not intended for general use and gives no API or ABI stability guarantee; HAProxy dropped BoringSSL support for that reason (no LTS cycle, no stable API).

ChaCha20-Poly1305 bulk encryption on AVX-512 CPUs: BoringSSL has no AVX-512 ChaCha20, and one cycle-count run (soda4fries/ChaChaCha, EPYC 9655 Zen 5) shows its AVX2 code at 1.52 cycles/byte vs OpenSSL's 0.84 for 16 KiB records (about 1.8x slower).

Code that needs OpenSSL APIs BoringSSL removed: there is no include/openssl/ocsp.h (OCSP request/response parsing, so nginx's ssl_stapling cannot fetch responses; stapling a caller-supplied response via SSL_CTX_set_ocsp_response does work), EVP_PKEY_HMAC is gone, DSA EVP_PKEYs cannot sign or verify, and server-side or DTLS renegotiation is unsupported.

If you need a documented RSA or ECDSA speedup over a current OpenSSL 3.x release: the only numbers comparing the two are a 2018 forum post against an OpenSSL 1.1.1 pre-release, and they are within about 10% either way.

integration.form: static lib (CMake or the Bazel Central Registry module; projects often vendor the source under third_party/boringssl/src with generated source lists from gen/; -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=1 gives a shared lib but without ABI stability)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime; CMake 3.22+ to build (Ninja recommended), NASM on Windows; Go (latest stable) and optionally libunwind only for the test suites
integration.min_toolchain: C11 and C++17 compilers; build tools no older than five years (Abseil policy); GCC 6.1+ or recent Clang on non-Windows; MSVC from Visual Studio 2022 with Windows 10 SDK 2104+
integration.platforms: x86-64, x86, AArch64 and ARMv7 with assembly fast paths (runtime CPU-feature dispatch on x86 and via getauxval on ARM Linux); Linux, macOS, Windows, iOS and Android documented; other targets fall back to C
integration.thread_safety: Initializes itself and uses pthreads or Windows primitives internally (OpenSSL locking callbacks are no-ops); per API-CONVENTIONS.md, key objects such as RSA or EVP_PKEY may be used from several threads at once provided no thread mutates them; consult each header for other types.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — mostly source-compatible with the OpenSSL 1.1.0 API subset it keeps (OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER matches, OPENSSL_IS_BORINGSSL marks it), but removed APIs, changed *_ctrl handling and integer types, and no ABI compatibility mean you rebuild and sometimes patch the consumer; it cannot replace a system libssl.so.

gotchas: Harness mismatch behind the 2018 numbers: bssl speed printed two RSA verify rows, 'verify (same key)' and 'verify (fresh key)'; the fresh-key row (tool/speed.cc at b579ecb, now bench/rsa.cc BM_SpeedRSAImportKeyAndVerify) rebuilds the public key and its Montgomery context on every call, while OpenSSL 1.1.1 'openssl speed' reuses one key. Comparing the fresh-key row with openssl speed understates BoringSSL, which likely explains why one summary has BoringSSL 8% faster at RSA-2048 verify and another 4.55% slower. The tools also differ in run length (bssl speed 1 s wall clock per row by default vs RSA_SECONDS/ECDSA_SECONDS 10 s) and RSA input (SHA-256 DigestInfo vs a raw 36-byte NID_md5_sha1 buffer); the ECDSA rows match (20-byte digest, same key, ECDSA_sign/ECDSA_verify).

The 'bssl speed' command used for the evidence no longer exists at HEAD: tool/tool.cc lists no speed subcommand and tool/speed.cc is gone from main; benchmarks moved to bench/*.cc and the bssl_bench binary on google/benchmark 1.9.4 (commit 23dec3c, Dec 2025), which by default runs every benchmark at 1 thread and at one thread per CPU.
Debug is the default CMake build (no optimization, assertions on); pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release before measuring anything.
Building for ARM with OPENSSL_STATIC_ARMCAP_* or -march features assumes those instructions exist at runtime; per BUILDING.md the binary will likely crash on CPUs that lack them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BoringSSL when you need a complete TLS stack with fast P-256, X25519, AES-GCM and ML-KEM in one maintained library; libsecp256k1 (secp256k1 only) and ENG25519 or the SUPERCOP Ed25519 code (single curves, research or reference code) beat OpenSSL by much larger, better-documented margins on their one primitive but provide no TLS.
verified_claims_summary: One centminmod forum user ran 'bssl speed' against 'openssl speed' from OpenSSL 1.1.1-pre9-dev on one unnamed machine in 2018 (no CPU, compiler or flags given; page unreachable here, read only through search snippets): RSA-2048 sign about 938.6 vs 923.6 ops/s (about 1.6% faster) and RSA-2048 verify 33663.8 vs 31108.1 ops/s with the same key (about 8% faster), both derived from snippet data; the ECDSA P-256 percentages could not be reproduced. A 2014 gist (Core i7 3630QM) shows BoringSSL about 1.14x faster per process at RSA-2048 sign and about 0.88x at verify against OpenSSL 1.0.1h, once OpenSSL's '-multi 2' totals are halved (derived from page data).
status_note: Very actively maintained by Google (security advisories through 2026-09-29, last commit 2026-10-11) and Apache-2.0, so copyable, but released only as git-head snapshots with no API/ABI stability; the evidence for beating OpenSSL is a snippet-only, single-machine 2018 comparison against an end-of-life development build.
